ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the Leiden University of Applied Sciences Research Ethics Committee (Reference: CEO 10/2024).

Participants were neurodivergent young people aged 11 to 23 years, recruited through multiple channels: advertisements on websites targeting neurodivergent groups, social media such as LinkedIn, the professional and personal networks of the researchers including contacts at residential facilities, and student-led recruitment as part of a course project at Leiden University of Applied Sciences.
For participants younger than 16 years, informed consent was obtained from parents or legal guardians.

Due to listwise deletion -not all participants completed the teacher questions -these analyses are based on a slightly reduced subsample, which accounts for the small difference in means compared to the analyses above.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

In an increasingly digitalized world, digital inclusion has become a key societal concern (Kargapolova et al., 2020).

text.text: However, neurodivergent youth, including those with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attentiondeficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), mild intellectual disabilities (MID), and dyslexia (Layinka et al., 2024), remain at risk of digital exclusion (Groot et al., 2022).

text.text: Digital technologies can enhance social participation, provide access to information, and support active citizenship, they may also expose these young people to distinct risks and vulnerabilities.
Many professionals and caregivers find it difficult to guide children in their digital lives (Gür & Türel, 2022; Nikken et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Many professionals and caregivers find it difficult to guide children in their digital lives <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Gür & Türel, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Nikken et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The pace of change in the digital world makes it difficult to keep up, and caregivers who lack digital skills find it difficult to connect with and guide young people online (Gür & Türel, 2022).
text.formatted: The pace of change in the digital world makes it difficult to keep up, and caregivers who lack digital skills find it difficult to connect with and guide young people online <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Gür & Türel, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: While children tend to adapt quickly to these changes and develop strong digital skills, they often fail to anticipate the consequences of their online actions (Vale et al., 2018).
text.formatted: While children tend to adapt quickly to these changes and develop strong digital skills, they often fail to anticipate the consequences of their online actions <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Vale et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: It has therefore been suggested that improving caregivers' digital literacy could help them become better guides of young people's digital media use (Banic & Orehovacki, 2024; Nikken & Opree, 2018).
text.formatted: It has therefore been suggested that improving caregivers' digital literacy could help them become better guides of young people's digital media use <ref type="bibr">(Banic & Orehovacki, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Nikken & Opree, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: However, digital literacy needs to be transferred into practice, which makes parenting style and digital support practices at least as important (Vossen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: However, digital literacy needs to be transferred into practice, which makes parenting style and digital support practices at least as important <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Vossen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Children need support in both online and offline settings, for example in navigating social interactions, managing risk-taking behaviors, and respecting boundaries.
Online and offline environments are not fundamentally different in this regard and often; youth might even consider them to be one and the same.
From this perspective, parental style, professional support and digital support practices may matter more than adults' digital literacy in managing children's digital behavior (Vossen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: From this perspective, parental style, professional support and digital support practices may matter more than adults' digital literacy in managing children's digital behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Vossen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: As online and offline environments are not fundamentally different, understanding effective digital support may benefit from insights into established parenting styles in offline contexts.
These styles are commonly characterized along two dimensions: demandingness and responsiveness (Baumrind, 2013).
text.formatted: These styles are commonly characterized along two dimensions: demandingness and responsiveness <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Baumrind, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: A parenting style that is high on demandingness and low on responsiveness is referred to as an 'authoritarian' parenting style.
When both demandingness and responsiveness are high, this is considered 'authoritative' parenting.
A combination of low demandingness and high responsiveness is called 'permissive' parenting.
Finally, a parenting style low on both demandingness and responsiveness is considered a 'neglectful' parenting style (Baumrind 2013).
text.formatted: Finally, a parenting style low on both demandingness and responsiveness is considered a 'neglectful' parenting style <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Baumrind 2013)</ref>.

text.text: In the digital field offline parenting styles were not directly incorporated.

Instead, much of the research on digital support styles builds on the three parental-mediation strategies originally identified by Bybee et al. (1982) for television and later refined by Valkenburg et al. (1999): restrictive mediation (setting rules and boundaries), instructive or active mediation (discussing media content with the child), and social co-viewing or co-use (watching/using media together without critically discussing it).
text.formatted: Instead, much of the research on digital support styles builds on the three parental-mediation strategies originally identified by <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bybee et al. (1982)</ref> for television and later refined by <ref type="bibr">Valkenburg et al. (1999)</ref>: restrictive mediation (setting rules and boundaries), instructive or active mediation (discussing media content with the child), and social co-viewing or co-use (watching/using media together without critically discussing it).

text.text: Building on this, a large cross-national study in eight countries by Livingstone et al. (2017) identified two broader support styles: 'enabling parenting', which combines active mediation together with control and monitoring creating a safe environment to encourage positive internet use, and 'restrictive parenting', which focusses on restrictions.

(2017)</ref> identified two broader support styles: 'enabling parenting', which combines active mediation together with control and monitoring creating a safe environment to encourage positive internet use, and 'restrictive parenting', which focusses on restrictions.

text.text: Although this framework was originally developed in the context of parental support, Mendoza (2009) argued that these mediation styles also apply to teachers and other professionals working with children.
text.formatted: Although this framework was originally developed in the context of parental support, <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Mendoza (2009)</ref> argued that these mediation styles also apply to teachers and other professionals working with children.

text.text: Various studies show that support style is generally associated with children's wellbeing and their engagement in risky behavior, although effects are often small and the resulting picture is nuanced.

For the offline world, Azman et al. (2021) found that both authoritative and permissive parenting styles were associated with better mental health scores in children and adolescents, while demanding-controlling and emotionally distancing styles showed the least favorable outcomes.

(2021)</ref> found that both authoritative and permissive parenting styles were associated with better mental health scores in children and adolescents, while demanding-controlling and emotionally distancing styles showed the least favorable outcomes.

text.text: In the digital domain, this would translate to support that combines support and trust with clear rules about media use. Geurts et al. (2023) found that a tolerant and supportive parenting profile (characterized by high responsiveness and autonomy-granting rather than strict rulesetting) predicted lower levels of problematic social media use over time than profiles combining high restrictions with either low or high support, with high restrictions and low support predicting the highest levels of problematic social media use, suggesting that a supportive general parenting context may matter more than internet-specific restrictions. Flamant et al. (2022) found that overprotective support was linked to maladjustment, aggression, and internalizing distress, though these effects were modest and depend partly on how adolescents cope with such parenting.

text.text: Some degree of parental control does appear to play a protective role.

Low levels of parental control were associated with excessive screen exposure (Coyne et al., 2017), and permissive or laissez-faire parenting was associated with greater involvement in cyberbullying as both victim and perpetrator (Vale et al., 2018).

text.text: Parental co-use and active involvement related to online risk-taking, particularly among boys (Notten & Nikken, 2016).
text.formatted: Parental co-use and active involvement related to online risk-taking, particularly among boys <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Notten & Nikken, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, Young and Tully (2022) found that autonomysupportive parenting, when combined with active mediation, had the most favorable outcomes: parents could best protect children from risky online experiences by supporting adolescent autonomy through open communication rather than through control alone.
text.formatted: In addition, <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Young and Tully (2022)</ref> found that autonomysupportive parenting, when combined with active mediation, had the most favorable outcomes: parents could best protect children from risky online experiences by supporting adolescent autonomy through open communication rather than through control alone.

text.text: Beyond individual caregivers, institutional settings may also shape children's digital behavior.
Schools in several countries have recently introduced smartphone bans, though the evidence on their effects remains inconclusive.
A meta-analysis of five studies found a significant but modest overall effect for social wellbeing (Böttger & Zierer, 2024).
text.formatted: A meta-analysis of five studies found a significant but modest overall effect for social wellbeing <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Böttger & Zierer, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A large observational study found that restrictive school phone policies were followed by reductions in phone and social media use during school hours but found no evidence of changes in use on weekdays or weekends, and no changes in overall mental wellbeing (Goodyear et al., 2025).
text.formatted: A large observational study found that restrictive school phone policies were followed by reductions in phone and social media use during school hours but found no evidence of changes in use on weekdays or weekends, and no changes in overall mental wellbeing <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Goodyear et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This suggests that school-based restrictions alone might be insufficient and that interventions should address both in-school and out-of-school screen use simultaneously, including effects on related behaviors such as sleep and physical activity.
All in all, these findings suggest that neither strict control nor unrestricted freedom is optimal.
Both responsiveness and appropriate demandingness contribute to reducing risky online behavior and promoting healthy digital engagement.
Children themselves recognize the value of parental rules and boundaries.

In a qualitative study, children across age groups agreed that rules were necessary and good for their safety and wellbeing, though older adolescents emphasized that rules should be negotiated rather than imposed (Nixon et al., 2010).
text.formatted: In a qualitative study, children across age groups agreed that rules were necessary and good for their safety and wellbeing, though older adolescents emphasized that rules should be negotiated rather than imposed <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Nixon et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The effects of support might also not be one-directional.
The way children respond to support may shape the support they receive.

Digital support is often described in a one-sided manner, focusing on the actions of caregivers whilst paying less attention to children's coping strategies and self-disclosure (Modecki et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Digital support is often described in a one-sided manner, focusing on the actions of caregivers whilst paying less attention to children's coping strategies and self-disclosure <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Modecki et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, support is inherently interactive: a caregiver's approach will shape the child's reaction, and vice versa.

Bidirectional effects were identified by De Groot et al. (2023) among professionals working with youth with mild intellectual disabilities, in which support was only provided when youth actively asked for help, making the child's initiative the starting point for support.

(2023)</ref> among professionals working with youth with mild intellectual disabilities, in which support was only provided when youth actively asked for help, making the child's initiative the starting point for support.

text.text: Active and open communication may encourage adolescent self-disclosure, while rule setting can lead to compliance but also to aggression, internalizing distress (Flamant et al. 2022) or technical workarounds such as moving to alternative platforms when certain apps are restricted (Modecki et al., 2022).

text.text: The benefits of youth involvement in rule-setting is age-dependent. should not be overstated, however. Geurts et al. (2025) found age-dependent effect of rule-setting on the onset of problematic social media use.

text.text: Effect of rules were strongly age-dependent: for younger adolescents, stricter rules were associated with a lower likelihood of developing problematic use, while for older adolescents -from around age 16 -stricter rules were associated with a higher likelihood.
This underscores the importance of age-appropriate support strategies.
Finally, caregivers should bear in mind that their own media use serves as a direct model for children's digital behavior (Geurts et al., 2022; Nikken, 2017).
text.formatted: Finally, caregivers should bear in mind that their own media use serves as a direct model for children's digital behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Geurts et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Nikken, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Teachers, professionals and caregivers might find it particularly challenging to find the right balance in digital support for neurodivergent children.
Digital support involves a complex balance between communicating trust, offering support and digital opportunities, while also setting boundaries and monitoring to prevent harm (Modecki et al. 2022).
text.formatted: Digital support involves a complex balance between communicating trust, offering support and digital opportunities, while also setting boundaries and monitoring to prevent harm <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Modecki et al. 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Parents of children with ASD, for example, more frequently offered digital devices as a strategy to help their child self-regulate during moments of distress compared to parents of typically developing children (Pliska et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Parents of children with ASD, for example, more frequently offered digital devices as a strategy to help their child self-regulate during moments of distress compared to parents of typically developing children <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Pliska et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, these neurodivergent children are more vulnerable to online risks such as addiction (Alper et al., 2023), requiring caregivers to navigate the tension between the potential benefits of digital media and its associated risks.
text.formatted: At the same time, these neurodivergent children are more vulnerable to online risks such as addiction <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Alper et al., 2023)</ref>, requiring caregivers to navigate the tension between the potential benefits of digital media and its associated risks.

text.text: Several studies support the need for a dual approach combining protection with engagement.
For children with ADHD, whose impulsivity makes them more prone to risk-taking behavior, monitoring online behavior is found to have a protective effect (Pollak et al. 2020).
text.formatted: For children with ADHD, whose impulsivity makes them more prone to risk-taking behavior, monitoring online behavior is found to have a protective effect <ref type="bibr">(Pollak et al. 2020)</ref>.

text.text: For autistic children, who tend to use screens more frequently and for longer periods, increasing their risk of screen addiction, limiting screen time is found to be particularly important (Yuan et al. 2024).
text.formatted: For autistic children, who tend to use screens more frequently and for longer periods, increasing their risk of screen addiction, limiting screen time is found to be particularly important <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Yuan et al. 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, Verhagen et al. (2025) found that resilience-oriented parenting was associated with increased externalizing symptoms in children with ADHD and ASD, suggesting limit-setting is important for caregivers of neurodivergent children.
text.formatted: Additionally, <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Verhagen et al. (2025)</ref> found that resilience-oriented parenting was associated with increased externalizing symptoms in children with ADHD and ASD, suggesting limit-setting is important for caregivers of neurodivergent children.

text.text: However, an overly restrictive approach might increase the risk of digital exclusion (Livingstone et al. 2017).
text.formatted: However, an overly restrictive approach might increase the risk of digital exclusion <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Livingstone et al. 2017)</ref>.

text.text: This underscores the need for a careful balance between protection and participation, a core principle of social work practice in offline settings (Veselinova, 2014).
text.formatted: This underscores the need for a careful balance between protection and participation, a core principle of social work practice in offline settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Veselinova, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: As digital technologies become more integrated into everyday life, this tension is increasingly reflected in the online world as well.
To better understand how a balance can be achieved between protection and participation, it is essential to consider children's own perspectives.
Despite a growing body of research on digital inclusion and online safety, relatively little is known about how children themselves experience and evaluate the digital support they receive.

Research on digital guiding styles has predominantly focused on caregivers' perceptions and less on the children's own views in which parents describe their children's media use and their own parenting styles (Alper et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2022; Livingstone et al. 2017).
text.formatted: Research on digital guiding styles has predominantly focused on caregivers' perceptions and less on the children's own views in which parents describe their children's media use and their own parenting styles <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Alper et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Lee et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Livingstone et al. 2017)</ref>.

text.text: This is a noticeable gap, as children have experiential views on what forms of support they find helpful or unhelpful in navigating their digital lives.
Children might not merely seek fewer boundaries, they are also aware that restrictions are sometimes necessary (Nixon et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Children might not merely seek fewer boundaries, they are also aware that restrictions are sometimes necessary <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Nixon et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: This is particularly relevant for neurodivergent children, whose specific vulnerabilities and needs may shape how they experience and evaluate the support they receive.
Hence, this study explored support styles applied by caregivers (parents and teachers) as experienced by neurodivergent children and forms of support they found most helpful.
This leads to the following research questions: Which digital support styles did youth perceive from their parents and teachers?
How effective did neurodivergent youth perceive digital support styles?
Did support styles differ by type of neurodivergence and self-perceived digital capabilities?
This study employed a cross-sectional quantitative design.

Participants were neurodivergent young people aged 11 to 23 years, recruited through multiple channels: advertisements on websites targeting neurodivergent groups, social media such as LinkedIn, the professional and personal networks of the researchers including contacts at residential facilities, and student-led recruitment as part of a course project at Leiden University of Applied Sciences.
Inclusion criteria were age between 11 and 23 and having a diagnosis of one or more types of neurodiversity or self-identifying as neurodivergent.
These criteria were verified through screening questions included in the online questionnaire.
Data collection took place between October 2024 and January 2025 using two methods.
Participants aged 16 years and older filled in an online questionnaire in Qualtrics.
Participants younger than 16 and those with MID filled in a similar questionnaire in a face-to-face setting with the support of a trained interviewer.
The interviews took place either at the participant's home or at the residential facility where the adolescent lived.
Data collection was conducted in accordance with scientific ethical regulations.
All participants and/or their parents or legal guardians were informed about the aim of the study, its voluntary nature, and the activities involved.
Participants aged 16 years and older provided consent through the questionnaire.
For participants younger than 16 years, informed consent was obtained from parents or legal guardians.
For participants with MID, healthcare professionals at the relevant facilities informed parents or guardians about the study and obtained consent on behalf of the research team.
Data collection commenced only after consent had been secured.
The study was approved by the Leiden University of Applied Sciences Research Ethics Committee (Reference: CEO 10/2024).

The questionnaire included questions about demographics, online activities, perceived need for support in online activities, support capabilities of parents, perceived internet self-esteem, digital capabilities, and parenting and support styles.
For participants younger than 16 years and those with MID some questions were removed and others were reworded to reduce cognitive load.
Below, only the measures relevant to the study aims are described.
To assess digital support styles, 13 items on guiding behaviors were developed by the first two authors (Table 1).

text.text: These were based on items used in a previous exploratory study (Nikken & Büttner, 2021) and adapted considering findings from further exploratory research by the second author (De Groot et al., 2023).

text.text: No priori dimensions were defined.
The items were for this study categorized according to the theoretical frameworks of Baumrind (2013) and Glatz et al. (2018).
text.formatted: The items were for this study categorized according to the theoretical frameworks of <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Baumrind (2013)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Glatz et al. (2018)</ref>.

text.text: Face validity and feasibility were assessed by the senior researchers of the research project group with expertise on the topic.
Participants indicated how often parents showed each of the 13 guiding behaviors, using a 4-point Likert-scale ranging from 'never' to 'very often'.
An example item was: "How often does your parent set limits (e.g., saying how long or how often you are allowed to use a screen)?"
Participants aged 16 and older answered the same questions twice: once with reference to their parents and once with reference to their teachers.
Participants aged 16 and older ranked the same 13 guiding behaviors from most to least effective, where a rank of 1 indicated the behavior perceived as the most effective and 13 the least effective.
To answer the research questions, we first examined the factor structure of the 13 digital support behaviors, after checking the distribution of items and inter-item correlations.
Items with consistently low correlations with all other items (r < .30) were considered for exclusion.
text.formatted: Items with consistently low correlations with all other items (r < .30) were considered for exclusion.

text.text: An exploratory factor analysis (EFA) with varimax rotation was conducted on the frequency of support behaviors as reported for parents.
The number of factors to retain was determined by inspecting eigenvalues greater than one and the scree plot, with theoretical considerations serving as the final criterion in case of ambiguity.
Items with low loadings on both factors were considered for exclusion.
Items with negative loadings were recoded prior to further analyses.

Based on the factor structure identified in the EFA for support by parents, we then assessed whether the same factor structure was applicable to support by teacher by examining the internal consistency of the resulting support style dimensions using McDonald's omega (Hayes & Coutts, 2020).
text.formatted: Based on the factor structure identified in the EFA for support by parents, we then assessed whether the same factor structure was applicable to support by teacher by examining the internal consistency of the resulting support style dimensions using McDonald's omega <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hayes & Coutts, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: For each participant, mean scores were calculated for the two identified support style dimensions.
Differences in the reported frequency of support styles between parents and teachers were examined using paired samples t-tests.

Differences in reported frequencies between groups based on type of neurodiversity were examined using independent samples t-tests, with each neurodiversity type compared separately against participants without that diagnosis.
To address the research questions on perceived effectiveness, analyses were conducted at two levels.
At the item level, descriptive statistics were calculated for each of the 13 support behaviors based on their rank-order scores.

At the support style level, differences in perceived effectiveness between the two support styles were examined using a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, given the ordinal nature of the ranking data and the paired structure of the comparisons.
All effects were teste on a significant p-level of p < 0.05.
text.formatted: All effects were teste on a significant p-level of p < 0.05.

text.text: The online questionnaire was started by 73 respondents aged 16 and older.
Of these, 21 completed only the demographic questions, one partially completed the questionnaire, and four identified as neurotypical.
These respondents were excluded from further analyses, resulting in a final online sample of 47 respondents.
The mean age of this group was 19.5 years (SD = 1.7).
The sample included 24 males (51%), 18 females (38%), three nonbinary participants (6%), one transmasculine participant (2%), and one participant who declined to disclose their gender (2%).
Ten participants (21%) were not in education at the time of the study.

Participants could report more than one neurodevelopmental condition. 19 participants (62%) reported ADHD, 13 (28%) reported dyslexia, 12 (26%) reported autism, four (9%) were identified as highly gifted, and one (2%) reported MID.
The participant with MID completed the full online questionnaire with interviewer support rather than the simplified version.
As excluding this participant did not substantially affect the results, they were retained in the final sample.
A visualization of the response flow is presented in Figure 1.
text.formatted: A visualization of the response flow is presented in Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore , 12 participants who were younger than 16 or reporting MID completed the questionnaire with the support of a researcher.
One did not complete the questionnaire and was excluded from further analyses, resulting in an in-personinterview sample of 11 participants.
The mean age of this group was 16.8 years (SD=4.9).
The group consisted of five boys (42%) and six girls (55%).
Eight participants (73%) were in education at the time of the study and three (27%) were not.
Of those in education, four attended special education, one primary school, one secondary school, and two vocational education.
Participants could report more than one neurodevelopmental condition.
Six participants (55%) reported MID, two (18%) reported dyslexia, two (18%) reported ADHD, one (9%) reported autism, and one (9%) was identified as highly gifted.
The items of the digital support frequency scale as answered for parents did not follow a normal distribution.
Some items showed positive skewedness, while others were negatively skewed.
This deviation from normality was taken into account when interpreting the results.
Although violations of normality may reduce the quality of the solution, factor analysis under these conditions is still considered informative (Tabachnick & Fidell, 2001).

text.text: Due to skewness, univariate outliers were identified but not excluded.

Inter-item correlation analyses revealed that the item "My parents do not know how to help me" showed consistently low correlations with all other items (r < .23) and was therefore excluded from further analyses, reducing the scale to 12 items.

text.text: Screening for multivariate outliers at the respondent level identified three multivariate outliers (χ²(12) > 32.91, p < .001).

text.text: Since excluding these respondents did not substantially alter the results, they were retained.
All reported results are therefore based on the full sample (N = 58).
An exploratory factor analysis with varimax rotation was conducted on the 12 remaining digital support behavior items as answered for parents.
The initial solution yielded four factors with eigenvalues greater than one.
However, inspection of the scree plot suggested a two-factor solution provided a better fit.
This two-factor solution was also more consistent with the theoretical framework on support styles described in the introduction and was therefore selected.
The two-factor solution accounted for 48.05% of the total variance.
Table 1 presents the items, factor loadings, and descriptive statistics.

text.text: Item 4 -"They watch when I do online activities.
They sit next to me while I am busy with things from everyday digital life." -showed low loadings on both factors (Factor1 = 0.15, Factor2 = 0.09) and was therefore removed from the scale.

This is consistent with Modecki et al. (2022), who noted that co-viewing items are of decreasing relevance to digital parenting, as they originate from an era of shared television and desktop computer use (Valkenburg et al., 1999) and no longer reflect the predominantly individual and mobile nature of children's digital activities.

(2022)</ref>, who noted that co-viewing items are of decreasing relevance to digital parenting, as they originate from an era of shared television and desktop computer use <ref type="bibr">(Valkenburg et al., 1999)</ref> and no longer reflect the predominantly individual and mobile nature of children's digital activities.

text.text: Item 3 -"They let me arrange it myself; I am allowed to try it myself"showed a negative loading on the first factor, indicating a reverse relation with the other items on that factor, and was recoded for subsequent analyses.

Based on item content and factor loadings, Factor 1 was interpreted as reflecting a restrictive and authoritarian support style, and Factor 2 as reflecting an enabling and authoritative support style.
Internal consistency of the two support style factors was examined using McDonald's omega.
For the responses on parent support, Factor 1 showed acceptable internal consistency (ω = .79), which increased only marginally when item 3 was deleted (ω = .81).
For Factor 2, internal consistency was questionable (ω = .68), and deleting items did not improve reliability.
Based on these results, all items were retained for the responses on parent support scale.
Participants aged 16 and older (N = 47) also reported how often their teachers applied the same support behaviors.

For the responses on teacher support, internal consistency for Factor 1 could not be computed when item 3 was included, as McDonald's omega assumes a unidimensional structure, an assumption that is likely violated when item 3 (which loaded negatively on Factor 1) is included.
When item 3 was deleted, internal consistency for Factor 1 was acceptable (ω = .79).
For Factor 2, internal consistency was questionable (ω = .63) and did not meaningfully improve when items were deleted.
Based on these findings and on item content, item 3 was deleted from all further analyses.

Although item 3 -"They let me arrange it myself; I am allowed to try it myself." -taps into the degree of autonomy children experience in their digital lives, it is conceptually ambiguous: a high score on this item does not necessarily reflect the opposite of restrictive parenting, and its inclusion undermined the unidimensionality of Factor 1.
It should be noted that the non-normal distribution of items may have affected the reliability estimates.
Skewed items tend to show reduced variance due to ceiling and floor effects, which can artificially lower McDonald's omega values.
The reliability estimates reported here should therefore be interpreted with this limitation in mind.

text.text: This study examined digital support styles as perceived by neurodivergent young people.
Support behaviors differed between an 'enabling and authoritative style' and a 'restrictive and authoritarian style'.
Both parents and teachers applied the enabling and authoritative style more frequently than the restrictive and authoritarian style.

When parents and teachers were compared directly, parents were reported to apply the enabling and authoritative style more frequently than teachers, while no significant difference was found for the restrictive and authoritarian style.
Some differences were found between neurodivergence types.
According to neurodivergent youth, parents of young people with MID applied a restrictive authoritarian style more frequently than parents of young people without MID.

In contrast, responses of the youth indicated that parents of young people with ADHD and dyslexia applied a restrictive authoritarian style less frequently than parents of young people without these conditions; a finding that warrants further interpretation and is discussed below.
Teachers applied an enabling authoritative style less frequently to young people with dyslexia than to those without dyslexia, as perceived by these young people.
With respect to perceived effectiveness, neurodivergent young people rated the enabling authoritative support style as significantly more effective than the restrictive authoritarian style.
At the item level, monitoring, removing media devices, and prohibiting digital content were perceived as least effective, while setting limits was considered moderately helpful.
Helping when asked, doing online activities together, and allowing young people to manage their own digital lives were perceived as most effective.
Among neurotypical youth evidence indicates that such a more autonomy-supportive style does benefit children's development (De Clercq et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Among neurotypical youth evidence indicates that such a more autonomy-supportive style does benefit children's development <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(De Clercq et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The finding that parents applied an enabling and authoritative support style more frequently than teachers, while no significant difference was found for the restrictive and authoritarian style, is consistent with theoretical distinctions between enabling and restrictive mediation strategies (Livingstone et al., 2017).

text.text: In educational settings, teachers' digital support tends to be organized around risk prevention, managing online behavior, and meeting institutional responsibilities -which may make rule-based and restrictive practices comparatively prominent (Berger, 2020; Chiner et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In educational settings, teachers' digital support tends to be organized around risk prevention, managing online behavior, and meeting institutional responsibilities -which may make rule-based and restrictive practices comparatively prominent <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Berger, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Chiner et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Parents, by contrast, can engage in more continuous day-to-day interaction with their children, which may create more opportunities for supportive, dialogical support and make such behaviors more visible to adolescents.
It is important to acknowledge, however, that the parent-teacher comparison in this study is only based on participants aged 16 and older.
There is a possibility that teachers use enabling and authoritative support more frequently in this younger group as these children still learn how to use and cope with digital media.
Several differences were found between neurodivergence types, although the small group sizes warrant cautious interpretation.
Parents of young people with MID were reported to apply a restrictive authoritarian support style more frequently than parents of young people without MID.
This finding is perhaps unsurprising given the cognitive vulnerabilities associated with MID, which may lead caregivers to prioritise protection and limit-setting.
While such an approach may offer short-term protection, overly restrictive support risks long-term digital exclusion (Livingstone et al., 2017).
text.formatted: While such an approach may offer short-term protection, overly restrictive support risks long-term digital exclusion <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Livingstone et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: If young people with MID are only controlled and protected, they might not have the opportunity to try things for themselves and learn from their own experiences and mistakes (Nowogrodzki, 2025; Sharman, 2014).
text.formatted: If young people with MID are only controlled and protected, they might not have the opportunity to try things for themselves and learn from their own experiences and mistakes <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Nowogrodzki, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Sharman, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Finding the right balance between protection and participation therefore takes courage but is particularly important for this group.
In contrast, parents of young people with ADHD and dyslexia applied a restrictive authoritarian support style less frequently than parents of young people without these conditions.
This is somewhat counterintuitive, given that both ADHD and dyslexia are associated with increased vulnerability to online risks.
One possible explanation is that parents of children with ADHD and dyslexia are more focused on supporting their child's autonomy and self-regulation.
In these conditions enabling support may be seen as more appropriate than restriction.
Finally, this study relied entirely on children's self-reported perceptions of the support they receive.
No caregiver data were collected to compare the perceptions of the children with those of the caregivers.
Future research would benefit from including both child and caregiver perspectives to obtain a more complete picture of digital support practices.

This study provides a first exploratory overview of digital support styles as perceived by neurodivergent young people, addressing a gap in the literature that has predominantly focused on caregivers' perspectives.

The findings show that neurodivergent young people experience enabling and authoritative support (combining support, open communication, and opportunities for autonomy) as more effective than restrictive and authoritarian approaches.

Monitoring, removing devices, and prohibiting digital content were perceived as least effective, while being helped when asked and having freedom to navigate digital life independently were valued most.

These findings are nuanced by differences between neurodivergence types and between parents and teachers and underscore the importance of incorporating children's own perspectives in research on and guidelines for digital support of neurodivergent young people.
This study demonstrates that neurodivergent young people's perceptions of digital support can be meaningfully studied by asking them to evaluate specific support behaviors.

Given that today's caregivers did not grow up navigating the same digital landscape as their children, incorporating young people's perspectives into guidelines and training materials is both feasible and valuable.
The findings might lead to direct implications for practice if replicated.
Neurodivergent young people perceive enabling and authoritative support as most effective.
At the same time, they recognise that some degree of boundary-setting is helpful.
These perceptions should inform guidelines for neurodivergent young people.

In particular, teachers appear to apply enabling and authoritative support less frequently than parents, suggesting that professional development in educational settings should explicitly encourage this approach.
By offering enabling rather than solely protective support, professionals, parents, and teachers can strengthen the digital participation of neurodivergent youth.
Increased participation may, in turn, promote access to information, social connectedness, and societal citizenship, contributing to greater digital inclusion.
Especially for young people with MID, the findings highlight the importance of moving beyond purely protective and restrictive approaches.
While the vulnerabilities of this group make caution understandable, overly restrictive support risks digital exclusion and limits opportunities for learning through experience.
Caregivers of young people with MID need to be supported in how to balance protection with participation.
Several directions for future research follow from these findings.
First, studies with larger and more diverse samples are needed to replicate and extend these findings, particularly for specific neurodiversity types where subgroup sizes were small.

Second, including a neurotypical comparison group would allow for a more direct examination of whether and how the support preferences of neurodivergent young people differ from those of their neurotypical peers.

Third, future research could collect data from both children and caregivers to examine the degree of alignment or misalignment between children's perceptions of support received and caregivers' accounts of support given.
Finally, longitudinal designs would allow researchers to examine whether support style predicts digital wellbeing and online risk-taking over time in neurodivergent populations.

text.text: With respect to teachers, young people with dyslexia reported receiving an enabling and authoritative support style from their teachers less frequently than young people without dyslexia.

Given that dyslexia is associated with specific challenges in online learning environments, the relative absence of enabling support from teachers for this group is a finding that deserves attention in educational practice.
Children with dyslexia benefit from online and digital tools such as text to speech editors.
This implies that these children might benefit a lot from more enabling and authoritative support (Raghavendra et al. 2018).

text.text: Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings.
First, not all participants received the same questionnaire or data collection procedure.
Participants aged 16 and older completed an online survey independently, while younger participants and those with MID completed a simplified questionnaire in a supported face-to-face interview.
These different modes of data collection may have influenced responses.
Faceto-face interviews can be susceptible to social desirability effects, potentially leading participants to present support as more positive than it was.
At the same time, the supported interview format may have enabled participants with MID to report their experiences more accurately than they could have in an unsupported online survey.
The extent to which mode effects influenced the findings is difficult to determine.
Second, the subgroup sizes for specific neurodiversity types were particularly limited and confounding factors such as gender or age could not be taken into account.

This reduces statistical power and means that null findings, such as the absence of significant differences for autism and high intellectual ability, should not be interpreted as evidence of no effect.
Conversely, significant findings based on small subgroups should be interpreted with caution.
Third, neurodivergent children's perceptions were not compared with those of neurotypical children.

While meaningful conclusions can be drawn about the experiences of neurodivergent young people themselves, no comparative statements about differences between neurodivergent and neurotypical children can be made on the basis of these data.
Fourth, the frequency of support behaviors showed skewed distributions with ceiling and floor effects, limiting variance.

While factor analysis is considered relatively robust to violations of normality (Tabachnick & Fidell, 2001), the reduced variance may have lowered statistical power in the group comparison analyses, potentially obscuring differences that exist in the broader population.
